title: A Correlate Is Not a Requirement

scenes.tts: A monkey watches a cloud of dots, some moving together and the rest at random. A neuron in its parietal cortex fires faster and faster. At a certain level, the monkey moves its eyes to answer. Is that neuron making the decision? Silence the area it sits in, and the monkey decides just as well.
scenes.visual: Dot cloud, a rising firing ramp to a level, an eye-movement chip; then the area is silenced and a question mark sits over the ramp.
scenes.narration: A monkey watches a cloud of dots, some moving together and the rest at random. A neuron in its parietal cortex fires faster and faster. At a certain level, the monkey moves its eyes to answer. Is that neuron making the decision? Silence the area it sits in, and the monkey decides just as well.

scenes.tts: Coherence is the percentage of dots that move together. Neurons in area M T are tuned to the direction of motion. In monkeys, each M T neuron was tested on a task matched to it. Most of the neurons studied discriminated motion about as well as the monkey, or better. Weak current into a small cluster of M T neurons with one preferred direction biased the monkeys' choices toward it. So M T supplies evidence, and its activity can sway the choice.

scenes.visual: Three dot panels at rising coherence, a direction tuning curve, a neuron-versus-monkey comparison, then current into a cluster shifting choices.

scenes.tts: The lateral intraparietal area, or L I P, holds neurons that fire before eye movements into their response field. Roitman and Shadlen let rhesus monkeys answer whenever they were ready. Stronger motion gave faster, more accurate choices, and L I P firing rose more steeply. It reached a similar level shortly before the eye movement, which the authors read as a threshold. These ramps are averages across trials, and whether single trials ramp or step is debated.

scenes.visual: Axes in this sketch; ramps of three slopes climb to a common dashed level, eye-movement ticks follow; a ramp-or-step question for single trials.

scenes.tts: A drift-to-bound model adds up evidence until the total hits a bound. In this invented example, with no noise, the rate starts at thirty spikes per second. It climbs to seventy after a latency of two hundred milliseconds, and the eye moves seventy milliseconds later. At fifty-one point two percent coherence the slope is four hundred, and the reaction time is three hundred seventy milliseconds. At twelve point eight percent it is six hundred seventy, and at three point two percent it is eighteen hundred seventy.
scenes.caption: A drift-to-bound model adds up evidence until the total hits a bound. In this invented example, with no noise, the rate starts at 30 spikes per second. It climbs to 70 after a latency of 200 milliseconds, and the eye moves 70 milliseconds later. At 51.2 percent coherence the slope is 400, and the reaction time is 370 milliseconds. At 12.8 percent it is 670, and at 3.2 percent it is 1,870.
scenes.visual: The ramp plot gets numbers: baseline 30, bound 70, 200 ms latency, three slopes, reaction-time markers at 370, 670 and 1,870 ms.

scenes.tts: Correlation shows what activity goes with a choice, but only a manipulation shows whether the choice needs it. Katz, Yates, Pillow and Huk silenced each area in turn in rhesus monkeys. They used muscimol, a drug that activates GABA A receptors. Silencing M T impaired motion discrimination. Silencing L I P produced no measurable impairment of motion decisions in the tasks tested.
scenes.caption: Correlation shows what activity goes with a choice, but only a manipulation shows whether the choice needs it. Katz, Yates, Pillow and Huk silenced each area in turn in rhesus monkeys. They used muscimol, a drug that activates GABA-A receptors. Silencing MT impaired motion discrimination. Silencing LIP produced no measurable impairment of motion decisions in the tasks tested.
scenes.visual: Two area boxes, each silenced in turn with muscimol; a discrimination meter drops for MT and holds for LIP.

scenes.tts: A missed injection could explain a null result, so the same monkeys did a free-choice task, with no right answer. After L I P inactivation, they chose targets in the affected part of space less often. Their eye movements to that side landed less accurately. The drug had acted, so L I P was not needed for this discrimination under those conditions. Keep this rule: a neuron that tracks a choice is not always needed for it.
